### day

**name:** Yusuf

**when:** A Tuesday in the school term

**where:** A South Asian city


**para**

- He is nineteen and has been at the madrasa since he was seven. He can recite the entire Qur'an. He cannot fill out the form at the government office where his brother works, because it is in English, and this is a fact he has known about himself for two years and has told no one.
- Morning revision at five. The younger boys sway over their texts. He loves this room. He loves the sound of it. He has been happy here in a way he does not think his brother has ever been happy anywhere.
- At nine Qari Sahib canes a boy named Bilal for the third time this month, on the hands, and the room goes carefully quiet and then resumes. Yusuf has seen this for twelve years. He no longer registers it as an event. Afterward Bilal sits beside him and Yusuf gives him half his bread and neither of them says anything.
- In the afternoon a man from the sponsoring foundation visits, and the boys line up, and there are photographs. The man's Arabic is better than the teachers'. Yusuf notices that the new books have arrived and that the new books say some things differently than the old books, and that nobody has remarked on this.
- At six he walks past the school his cousin attends, the one with the computer room. He stands there for a moment. Then he goes home, where his mother has made his favourite thing, and where his father says with real pride that his son is a hafiz and that Allah has blessed this house.
- At night on the roof he does something he does not do in front of anyone: he opens his brother's old English primer and works through eight words with a torch. It takes him forty minutes. He puts it back exactly where he found it. He is not certain whether what he is doing is ambition or betrayal, and there is nobody in the building he could ask.



## Shia Islam
*Abrahamic — Islamic*


### Opening

Karbala is in your body. The grief is not manipulation — it is one of the most morally serious things any religion has ever produced: a permanent memorial to refusing a corrupt ruler. Which is exactly why it matters who is standing on it now, and what they are collecting.


### Overview

~10–13% of Muslims, majority in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain; centered on devotion to the Prophet's family and the Imams, with a uniquely structured clerical hierarchy.


### Origin

Rooted in the succession claim of Ali and the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala (680 CE); the Twelver clerical hierarchy (marjaʿiyya) developed independent financial power through religious taxes; 1979 Iran fused the hierarchy with a state.


### authority

- The marjaʿiyya: senior ayatollahs whom believers must emulate (taqlid); in Iran, velayat-e faqih places a cleric atop the state itself.
- Clerical students and networks bound to marjas through stipends funded by religious taxes — a self-financing hierarchy unusual in Islam. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]


### money

- Khums: a 20% tax on surplus income, half of which (sahm-e Imam) is paid to the marjaʿ — direct, doctrine-mandated revenue to individual clerics' offices, largely unaudited. [OFFICIAL POLICY: fiqh manuals]
- In Iran, bonyads (revolutionary religious foundations) and shrine conglomerates like Astan Quds Razavi control vast tax-exempt economic empires answerable to the Supreme Leader, not parliament. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT / ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Pilgrimage economies: Karbala, Najaf, Mashhad, Qom.


### exit

- In Iran: state apparatus enforces religious compliance (morality policing, apostasy/blasphemy exposure). [GOVERNMENT REPORT: UN human rights reporting]
- Diaspora and communal costs mirror Sunni patterns; leaving devotional culture reads as betraying Husayn and family dead.


### whoBenefits

- The Iranian state and its clerical-security elite: religion as constitution, bonyads as off-budget wealth, martyrdom narrative as mobilization fuel. [ACADEMIC SOURCE / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Marjaʿ offices collecting khums with hereditary-adjacent succession of networks.
- Ritual economies around mourning seasons and shrine cities.


### healthy

- The quietist school (e.g., Sistani's Najaf) explicitly rejecting clerical rule; Iranian clerics and laity dissenting at enormous personal cost; the tradition's own resource: Karbala as a template for resisting corrupt power, including clerical power.


### timeline

- 632–661 CE — Succession claim of Ali; partisans of the House form — Authority is tied to lineage and designated knowledge, not consensus.
- 680 — Karbala: Husayn killed by Umayyad forces — Martyrdom becomes the tradition's emotional and moral center — and a permanent mobilizing engine.
- 874 — Occultation of the Twelfth Imam begins — Authority passes to scholars as deputies — creating the clerical class that still governs.
- 1501 — Safavid Iran adopts Twelver Shiism as state religion — The tradition acquires a state and a state-funded hierarchy.
- 1700s–1800s — Usuli school prevails; marjaʿiyya and khums collection consolidate — Clerics gain an independent revenue stream — self-financing religious power.
- 1890s–1970s — Clerical involvement in Iranian constitutional and nationalist politics — The hierarchy learns to move mass publics.
- 1979 — Iranian Revolution; velayat-e faqih installs clerical rule — For the first time, a jurist rules a modern state as a matter of constitutional law. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 1980s–2000s — Bonyads and shrine conglomerates expand; transnational networks grow — Off-budget religious economies answerable to the Leader alone. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- 2003–present — Post-Saddam Najaf revival; Sistani's quietist authority — A living demonstration that the tradition's own mainstream rejects clerical rule.
- 2017–present — Mass protests in Iran and Iraq against clerical governance, including by believers — Internal dissent is religious, not merely secular — the most important fact for readers to hold. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]


### demographics

**adherents:** ~180–250 million (~10–13% of Muslims). [ACADEMIC SOURCE: Pew]

**regions:** Iran (majority), Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Lebanon; large minorities in Pakistan, India, Afghanistan, Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, Kuwait, Yemen (Zaydi).

**branches:** Twelver (vast majority), Ismaili (including Nizari under the Aga Khan), Zaydi; within Twelver, quietist (Najaf) and activist/state (Qom) currents.

**trend:** Stable to growing with population; the political prestige of clerical rule has declined markedly among young Iranians. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**participation:** In Iran, state enforcement makes measurement unreliable — declared observance and private practice diverge sharply. Ritual participation (Muharram) far exceeds clerical obedience.


### info

- In Iran, religious authority and state censorship are the same apparatus: banned books, filtered internet, jailed journalists, and clerical courts. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Marjaʿ-following (taqlid) routes practical religious questions through a single office; changing marjaʿ is permitted, but the framework itself is not up for debate.
- Criticism of clerical rule is framed as serving foreign enemies — a nationalist inoculation against internal dissent. [LEADERSHIP STATEMENT]


### children

- Mourning rituals introduce children to grief narratives very young; in some contexts children participate in self-flagellation practices that senior clerics themselves have discouraged. [LEADERSHIP STATEMENT]
- In Iran, school curricula, hijab rules for girls from age 7 in the school setting, and ideological instruction are state-mandated. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Seminary tracks recruit adolescents into stipend-dependent careers that make later dissent economically ruinous.


### gender

- Compulsory hijab enforced by morality police in Iran; the death of Mahsa Amini in custody (2022) and the protest wave that followed made the enforcement machinery undeniable. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Temporary marriage (mutʿa) is doctrinally permitted and is used both consensually and, per critics, to legitimize exploitation. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Legal asymmetries in testimony weight, inheritance, custody, and travel permissions where religious law is state law. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Same-sex relations are capital offenses under Iranian law. [OFFICIAL POLICY / GOVERNMENT REPORT]


### moneyTable

- Khums (20% of surplus), half paid as sahm-e Imam — Support the Imam's portion and the poor — Doctrine-mandated payment directly to a cleric's office with no external audit — Marjaʿ offices, seminaries, clerical networks [OFFICIAL POLICY: fiqh manuals]
- Bonyads and shrine conglomerates — Charitable and revolutionary foundations — Tax-exempt commercial empires outside parliamentary oversight — Iran's clerical-security elite [ACADEMIC SOURCE / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Shrine pilgrimage economies (Karbala, Najaf, Mashhad, Qom) — Devotional visitation — Vast unaudited donation flows and adjacent commercial monopolies — Shrine administrations and appointed custodians
- Seminary stipends — Support religious study — Financial dependency of thousands of students on the hierarchy's goodwill — The hierarchy's continuity


### exitTable

- State punishment (Iran) — Yes — Morality policing, apostasy exposure, imprisonment of critics — “These are national security matters.”
- Family and community — Yes — Devotional culture is family-centered; leaving reads as betraying the martyrs — “Nobody forces belief in Shiism.”
- Livelihood — Yes for clerics and seminarians — Loss of stipend, housing, and status — “They chose another path.”
- Spiritual threat — Yes — Loss of intercession of the Imams; eternal consequence — “A statement of doctrine, not a threat.”


### whoPays

- Iranian women, under compulsory dress and unequal personal-status law.
- Protesters and dissenters, including devout ones, killed and imprisoned since 2017. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Baháʼís, Sunnis, and other minorities in Iran facing systematic discrimination.
- LGBTQ Iranians, under capital statutes.
- Ordinary payers of khums, funding offices they cannot audit.


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Low — In Iran the control is constitutional and statutory — the receipts are published law.
- Informal enforcement — Medium — Outside Iran, family and community devotion carries the enforcement.
- Leadership distance — Medium — Marjaʿ offices can disclaim the state; the state can disclaim any single marjaʿ.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Medium — Quietist versus activist readings let each disown the other's consequences.
- Cultural outsourcing — Medium — Enforcement attributed to Iranian culture or to security policy rather than religion.
- Volunteer enforcement — High — Basij-style volunteer enforcement and family policing are structural features.
- Sacred secrecy — Medium — Clerical courts and shrine finances operate without public disclosure.
- Exit cost denial — Medium — Officially belief is free; the penal code and the morality police are the correction.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Khums paid directly to a cleric's office

**origin:** Developed as the Usuli school prevailed in the 18th–19th centuries: half of the 20% levy (sahm-e Imam) goes to the marjaʿ as the Imam's deputy. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** With no Imam present and no state support, the hierarchy needed independent funding to remain free of kings. It worked — Shia clergy were financially independent precisely because ordinary people paid them directly.

**expired:** The mechanism now funds a hierarchy that in one country *is* the state. Independence from rulers was the entire justification; when the marjaʿ rules the country, the justification is gone and only the revenue remains.

**benefitsNow:** Marjaʿ offices and their networks, unaudited. You pay a fifth of your surplus to an institution that will not show you a ledger.

**mechanism:** Velayat-e faqih — clerical rule

**origin:** A minority juristic position elevated to constitutional principle in 1979. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** Presented as protection from a corrupt Western-backed monarchy. Many devout people believed it, and the grievance was real.

**expired:** After four decades the question is empirical, not theoretical: the arrangement produced morality police, prison sentences for journalists, and off-budget economic empires. The quietist Najaf school — the tradition's own mainstream — rejects it, which settles the claim that this is simply Shiism.

**benefitsNow:** A clerical-security elite governing bonyads and shrine conglomerates outside parliamentary oversight. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**mechanism:** Martyrdom devotion as political mobilization

**origin:** Karbala mourning (680 CE) as devotional and moral practice; converted into state mobilization infrastructure after 1979. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Remembering that a righteous man refused an unjust ruler and paid for it. A template for resisting power.

**expired:** Inverted. The commemoration of resistance to a corrupt ruler is now administered by the ruler. Grief for Husayn is used to recruit for state projects — an exact reversal of the story's meaning.

**benefitsNow:** The state and its military structures. Your tears are a mobilization asset, and the man you weep for died refusing exactly this.

**mechanism:** Compulsory hijab and morality policing

**origin:** State enforcement apparatus built after 1979; no classical precedent for police checking women's hair. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** None religious. It was a visible loyalty test for a new regime consolidating control of public space.

**expired:** A young woman died in custody over it in 2022 and the country rose, including believers. When enforcement kills the person it claims to protect, the claim is finished. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]

**benefitsNow:** The state's control of public space, and the security bodies employed to patrol it.

### leverage

- Iranian bonyads and shrine conglomerates — including one of the largest economic entities in the country — are tax-exempt, answerable to the Supreme Leader rather than parliament, and financed by devotional giving. Religion is the balance sheet. [ACADEMIC SOURCE / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Transnational religious-social networks provide clinics, schools, and welfare in other countries, and the provision converts into political influence over those communities. Aid that arrives with an ideology attached is not neutral aid. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Shrine city pilgrimage economies — Karbala, Najaf, Mashhad, Qom — move enormous unaudited sums through administrations appointed from above. [FINANCIAL RECORD]


### hardQuestions

- You pay a fifth of your surplus income to an office. Ask for the accounts. Then ask why the request itself is treated as impertinent.
- Husayn died refusing an unjust ruler. Explain how a system in which the ruler is the chief jurist is not the thing he refused.
- If clerical rule is Islam, why does Najaf — the tradition's senior center — reject it?
- A woman died in the custody of officers enforcing a religious rule. Which cleric lost his position over it?
- Why are the largest economic entities in a religious state exempt from the parliament its citizens elect?
- You were taught that internal criticism serves foreign powers. Notice that this is the exact argument Yazid's court would have made.


### closing

- No tradition in this codex has a better internal weapon than yours. Karbala is not a story about obedience; it is a story about a man who looked at overwhelming religious-political authority and said no, and lost, and was right. That is your inheritance, and it does not belong to the government.
- You can weep every Muharram and refuse every man who monetizes it. In fact, if the story means anything, that is what it requires.

### loopHere

**1:** Khums funds the seminaries that train the clerics who teach that khums is owed, to offices that publish nothing.

**2:** Loss of the Imams' intercession installed as the cost of leaving; relief through devotional participation; parents transmit it.

**3:** State curriculum, seminary stipends, and school dress rules attach identity before evaluation and make dissent unaffordable.

**4:** Transnational welfare networks deliver clinics and schools abroad and convert them into political influence.

**5:** Devotional giving and shrine labor build conglomerates that answer to one appointed office.

**6:** An enforcement death produces a temporary relaxation, not a change in the enforcement authority.

**7:** Real persecution of Shia populations elsewhere is invoked to reframe Iranian protesters as foreign agents.

**predict:** The next enforcement death will produce a period of visible leniency, a commission, and no change to who holds the power.


### day

**name:** Nasrin

**when:** A Tuesday in Muharram

**where:** Tehran


**para**

- The black banners have been up for a week. She loves Muharram. She has loved it since she was small enough to be carried through it, and the grief in it is not performed for her — it is the realest thing her calendar contains.
- She leaves for the university at seven-forty and checks her scarf in the lift mirror, and adjusts it, and checks it again, and this takes eleven seconds and happens every single day of her life and she has never once counted it before.
- In the seminar a lecturer says something careful about the economy and then, a beat later, says something more careful. Two students exchange a look. Nasrin writes down neither sentence.
- At lunch her friend Sahar shows her a photograph on a phone held low: a girl they were at school with, in a hospital bed, from the protests in the autumn. Sahar puts the phone away after four seconds. They eat their rice. Nasrin says, eventually, *does her mother know* and Sahar says *her mother is the one who sent it.*
- In the evening the majlis. The reciter's voice does the thing it does, and the room breaks, and Nasrin cries the way everyone cries, for Husayn, who stood in front of a ruler who claimed God's authority and refused him and was killed for it. She means every tear.
- Walking home her father talks about khums, which is due, and about which office they follow, and Nasrin asks — lightly, as a joke almost — whether anyone ever sees where it goes. Her father laughs and says that is not a question one asks. He is a kind man. He is not warning her. He simply does not have the question available, and she watches herself decide not to ask it again.



## Judaism
*Abrahamic*


### Opening

Your tradition puts its arguments in the canon. The Talmud preserves the losing opinion on the same page as the winning one — which means you were raised inside a religion that formally believes disagreement belongs in the record. Use that. Almost nothing in this profile asks you to be less Jewish; most of it asks you to be more.


### Overview

~15–16 million Jews worldwide, concentrated in Israel and the U.S.; a covenantal tradition of peoplehood, law, text study, and memory spanning Reform to Orthodox expressions.


### Origin

Ancient Israelite religion → Second Temple Judaism → rabbinic Judaism after the Temple's destruction (70 CE); the diaspora made community self-governance (kehilla) the institutional form; modernity fragmented practice into denominations; 1948 added a state with an official rabbinate.


### authority

- Decentralized: rabbis, communal boards, denominational bodies; no global hierarchy.
- In Israel, the Chief Rabbinate holds legal monopoly over Jewish marriage, divorce, conversion, and burial — state-enforced Orthodox gatekeeping over personal status for all Jewish citizens. [OFFICIAL POLICY]


### money

- Synagogue dues, day-school tuition (a defining family cost), kosher certification fees, federation philanthropy, Israel-linked giving.
- Kashrut certification is a genuine service and also a gatekeeping revenue economy for certifying agencies. [FINANCIAL RECORD]


### exit

- From liberal communities: low institutional cost. From Orthodox communities: see next profile.
- The agunah problem: because Jewish divorce requires the husband's grant of a get, recalcitrant husbands can chain wives indefinitely — rabbinic courts control the remedy. [ACADEMIC SOURCE / COURT RECORD]


### whoBenefits

- Israel's Chief Rabbinate and religious parties: state salaries, budgets, and coalition leverage in exchange for political support. [OFFICIAL POLICY / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Certification agencies; communal gatekeepers of conversion and status.


### healthy

- Judaism's argument culture: dissent preserved in the canon itself; independent minyanim, denominational pluralism, org-level transparency norms in federation philanthropy; activist rabbis pressuring the get system from within.


### timeline

- c. 1200–586 BCE — Israelite religion; monarchy; First Temple — Priesthood, sacrifice, and a centralized cult tied to a state.
- 586–539 BCE — Babylonian exile — Portable religion invented under catastrophe: text, law, and community replace territory.
- 516 BCE–70 CE — Second Temple period; sects (Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes) — Competing authorities; interpretation becomes the contested ground.
- 70 CE — Temple destroyed; rabbinic Judaism emerges at Yavneh — Priests are replaced by scholars — authority becomes textual and portable.
- 200–600 CE — Mishnah and Talmud compiled — Law codified in an argument format that preserves dissent inside the canon itself.
- 600–1500 — Diaspora kehilla self-governance under Muslim and Christian rule — Communities hold real coercive power over members (bans, taxes, courts) as the price of tolerated autonomy.
- 1700s–1800s — Hasidism; Haskalah; Reform movement; emancipation — Modernity splits Judaism into denominations with rival authority claims.
- 1881–1945 — Mass migration; Zionism; the Holocaust — Catastrophe and statehood reshape every institution and every argument about them.
- 1948 — State of Israel; Chief Rabbinate given legal monopoly over personal status — Religious authority acquires state enforcement for the first time in 1,900 years. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 1970s–present — Feminist and egalitarian movements; ordination of women in liberal denominations; agunah advocacy — Internal reform proceeds precisely where authority is not state-backed.


### demographics

**adherents:** ~15–16 million. [ACADEMIC SOURCE: Pew, DellaPergola demographic studies]

**regions:** Israel (~7M) and the United States (~6M) hold the large majority; France, Canada, UK, Argentina, Russia, Australia follow.

**branches:** Orthodox (Modern Orthodox and Haredi/Hasidic), Conservative/Masorti, Reform/Progressive, Reconstructionist, secular-cultural, plus Sephardi/Mizrahi and Ethiopian traditions cutting across.

**trend:** Overall slow growth; sharp internal shift — Haredi communities grow rapidly by fertility while liberal denominations shrink and intermarry.

**participation:** Identity is ethnic, cultural, and religious at once. A large share of Jews worldwide are secular or minimally observant; institutional authority reaches only a fraction, mainly through Israel's personal-status law and Orthodox communal structures.


### info

- In liberal denominations, information control is minimal — critical scholarship is taught in seminaries. This is a genuine asymmetry worth stating plainly.
- In Israel, the Rabbinate's monopoly means the state itself restricts which weddings, conversions, and burials legally exist — control of records, not of reading. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Communal reputation pressure discourages public discussion of abuse or of internal politics, particularly where donors and institutions overlap. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### children

- Circumcision at eight days; naming rites; day-school and supplementary-school education attach identity early.
- Bar/bat mitzvah at 12–13 marks legal obligation — a genuine coming-of-age rite that also formalizes duty before adult consent.
- Day-school tuition is a defining economic pressure on Jewish families, and it binds parents to institutions financially. [FINANCIAL RECORD]
- Youth movements and Israel trips build identity through peak experience — powerful, and in some programs explicitly designed to shape political and marital choices. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]


### gender

- The agunah problem is the tradition's sharpest live coercion issue: Jewish divorce requires the husband to grant a get, and rabbinic courts control the remedy. Women have been chained for years. [ACADEMIC SOURCE / COURT RECORD]
- Orthodox women cannot serve as witnesses, judges, or (in most streams) rabbis; mechitza seating and prayer-quorum exclusion are standard.
- Niddah (menstrual separation) and mikveh practice place intimate life under halachic supervision — experienced by many as meaningful, and as surveillance by others.
- Liberal denominations ordain women and LGBTQ clergy and perform same-sex marriage; Orthodoxy generally does not. The contrast is the clearest natural experiment in this codex.


### moneyTable

- Synagogue dues and High Holiday tickets — Fund the congregation — Paid access to worship at the year's most emotionally loaded moment; the poor self-exclude — Congregations (many now offer sliding scales — a real reform)
- Day-school tuition — Jewish education — Families locked into six-figure cumulative costs; institutional leverage over parents — Schools and community networks
- Kashrut certification — Reliable dietary supervision — Fee-based gatekeeping over an entire food economy; competing agencies with overlapping claims — Certifying agencies and their supervisors [FINANCIAL RECORD]
- Federation and mega-donor philanthropy — Communal welfare and Israel support — Large donors shape communal policy and speech norms disproportionately — Institutions and their major funders [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### exitTable

- Family and community (liberal streams) — Usually low — Ordinary relational friction; no formal sanction — Accurately: leaving really is low-cost here.
- Personal status (Israel) — Yes — Marriage, divorce, and burial run through the Rabbinate regardless of belief — “It's a civil arrangement, not coercion.”
- Marriage freedom (agunah) — Yes — Get refusal; rabbinic courts hold the only remedy — “The court cannot force a husband.”
- Conversion recognition — Yes — Non-Orthodox conversions rejected for Israeli personal-status purposes — “Standards, not exclusion.”


### whoPays

- Agunot — women denied divorce, sometimes for decades.
- Israelis of any belief who cannot marry, divorce, or be buried outside Rabbinate control.
- Converts whose status is questioned or revoked by later authorities.
- LGBTQ Jews in Orthodox communities.
- Families crushed by day-school tuition.
- Abuse survivors in institutions where donor and communal reputation outweighed reporting.


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Low in Israel — The Rabbinate's monopoly is statute — a published receipt. Elsewhere, halachic codes are open texts.
- Informal enforcement — Medium — Communal reputation and marriage networks carry pressure in observant circles.
- Leadership distance — High — Decentralization means no body is answerable for another's rulings.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Medium — Halachic pluralism allows any single ruling to be presented as one opinion among many.
- Cultural outsourcing — Medium — Family expectations and 'Jewish continuity' framing absorb responsibility.
- Volunteer enforcement — Medium — Community members enforce marriage and observance norms socially.
- Sacred secrecy — Medium — Institutional reputation management around abuse; batei din proceedings are private.
- Exit cost denial — Low outside Israel — Honest answer: in liberal Judaism, exit is genuinely cheap — the codex should say so.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Husband's exclusive power to grant divorce (the get)

**origin:** Deuteronomic and rabbinic marriage law, in which the man effects the divorce. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** In an ancient legal world where women could not contract, the framework at least required a formal written document rather than mere abandonment — a limit on male power at the time.

**expired:** Women now hold every legal capacity men do, except this one. The result is the agunah: a woman chained for years by a spiteful husband while rabbinic courts declare themselves unable to act.

**benefitsNow:** Recalcitrant husbands, who acquire indefinite leverage over a woman's entire future. And courts that retain the sole remedy and decline to use it decisively.

**mechanism:** State-enforced rabbinic monopoly on personal status (Israel)

**origin:** Ottoman millet arrangements carried into British Mandate law and then into Israeli statute in 1948. [OFFICIAL POLICY]

**thenPurpose:** Under empires, communal self-governance was how a minority survived with any autonomy at all.

**expired:** There is now a sovereign Jewish state with courts and a legislature. Retaining the monopoly means a secular Israeli, or a Reform convert, cannot marry, divorce, or be buried without Orthodox permission — religious authority backed by police power.

**benefitsNow:** The Chief Rabbinate and religious parties, who hold budgets and coalition leverage in exchange for political support. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]

**mechanism:** Mesirah — the prohibition on informing to secular authorities

**origin:** Medieval Europe, where handing a Jew to Christian authorities frequently meant torture, expropriation, or death. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Genuine protection. The gentile courts were not neutral; they were often the danger.

**expired:** Completely. Modern police forces in democratic states are not medieval blood-libel tribunals. Applying a rule built for pogrom conditions to a child-abuse allegation in Brooklyn protects only one party, and it is not the child. Rabbis have ruled internally that abuse reporting is not mesirah. [COURT RECORD]

**benefitsNow:** Abusers, and institutions whose reputations survive the silence. This is the clearest case in the codex of a genuinely protective rule outliving its threat and becoming the threat.

**mechanism:** High Holiday tickets and synagogue dues

**origin:** Voluntary communal taxation in self-governing kehillot, formalized as dues in the modern congregation. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** A community with no state funding taxed itself to pay for schools, burial, welfare, and courts.

**expired:** The welfare functions largely moved to the state and to federations, but the pricing remained — and it is heaviest at the year's most emotionally loaded moment. Many congregations now use sliding scales, which is real reform and worth naming.

**benefitsNow:** Congregational budgets. The cost is paid by the people who quietly stop coming because they cannot afford Yom Kippur.


### cycle


##### IDEALIZE

**does:** Creates emotional dependency before a single term, cost, obligation, or exit penalty has been disclosed.

2

**name:** HOOK

**essence:** You are given a future that cannot be verified, and a rope for whenever you drift toward the door.

### leverage

- Israel's religious parties convert a communal bloc vote into state budgets, draft exemptions, and control of personal status law for all Jewish citizens regardless of belief — religious authority purchased with coalition arithmetic. [OFFICIAL POLICY / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Major donors and federations shape communal policy and speech norms disproportionately; institutions dependent on a handful of funders learn what not to say. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Kashrut certification is a genuine service and a fee economy with competing agencies whose overlapping claims generate revenue rather than clarity. [FINANCIAL RECORD]


### hardQuestions

- A woman has been refused a get for six years. Name the rabbinic authority who has publicly declared her husband's conduct a violation and imposed a consequence. If you cannot, ask why not.
- If mesirah does not apply to child abuse — and prominent rabbis have said it does not — why do families who call the police still lose their standing?
- In a sovereign Jewish state, why does a secular Jew need Orthodox permission to marry, and which voter chose that?
- Why is a conversion valid in one country and void in another, and whose authority does that difference actually serve?
- If your community's institutions have nothing to hide, ask for the abuse-reporting policy in writing. Note how long it takes.
- You were taught that criticism helps antisemites. Ask who benefits from the rule that Jews may not say true things in public.


### closing

- The most Jewish response available to this material is argument, not offense. Your tradition canonized dissent, produced the prophets who screamed at kings, and preserved minority opinions for two thousand years in case they turned out to be right. Nothing here is foreign to that. The agunah advocates, the abuse reformers, the rabbis who ruled that reporting is not informing — they are doing exactly what the tradition trained them to do.
- Keep the arguing. Keep the Shabbat table. And notice that the parts of Judaism where exit is cheapest are also the parts where nobody had to be coerced into staying — which tells you something about what the coercion was ever for.

### loopHere

**1:** Dues, tuition, and certification fees fund the institutions that define the obligations, and the definitions do not shrink.

**2:** In observant communities, fear of communal standing does the work; in liberal ones this loop barely runs, which is the evidence.

**3:** Day schools and youth movements form identity early, and the tuition binds the parents to the institution financially.

### day

**name:** Rachel

**when:** A Tuesday in Elul

**where:** A North American suburb


**para**

- Carpool at 7:20 for the day school, which costs $34,000 a year for two children, which is more than the mortgage. She and David have run these numbers so many times that the numbers have stopped meaning anything and have become a kind of weather they live in.
- At the school gate she talks to Shira, who is on her fourth year of a get refusal. Shira's husband will not sign. The beit din has said what it says, which is that it cannot compel him. Shira is thirty-eight and cannot remarry and has stopped explaining this to people because of the particular face they make. Rachel hugs her and drives to work and grips the wheel at a red light.
- Her office is not Jewish and this is restful in a way she does not admit. Nobody here knows what a beit din is. Nobody here would understand that a woman she likes is legally chained to a man by a religious court that has a remedy it declines to use.
- At lunch she reads an email from the federation about the annual campaign, and a second email about a program that has been quietly discontinued, and she knows from communal gossip which donor did not like it. She replies to neither.
- Friday is coming, and Friday is the reason. The table, the candles, her daughter's hands over her eyes doing the blessing she learned at three. The argument with her brother that will run from the soup to the dessert and that both of them enjoy. Two thousand years of people arguing on the same page.
- At eleven she is doing the tuition spreadsheet again and David says, from the doorway, *we could send them to public school* and Rachel says *we could* and neither of them means it, and they both know why, and it isn't God. It's that the girls' entire world is at that school, and everyone they will ever marry is there, and this is how it works, and she does not have a word for how it works.



## Orthodox / Hasidic Judaism
*Abrahamic — Jewish*


### Opening

You may have the warmest community in the Western world. Real mutual aid, neighbors who show up, almost no loneliness — those things are true and this codex will not pretend otherwise. But you also live in the one community here where identity and institution are the same object, which means the cost of a single honest question is higher for you than for almost anyone else reading this.


### Overview

Traditionalist and ultra-Orthodox (Haredi/Hasidic) communities emphasizing full halachic observance; the fastest-growing Jewish population segment due to birth rates.


### Origin

Hasidism arose in 18th-century Eastern Europe around charismatic rebbes and dynastic courts; post-Holocaust reconstruction in Brooklyn, Jerusalem, and elsewhere rebuilt total communities with intentional insulation.


### authority

- Rebbes (dynastic, lifetime, hereditary) and poskim; modesty committees and communal enforcement; rabbinic courts (batei din) adjudicating internal disputes with strong norms against secular courts (mesirah taboo). [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Control of schools, matchmaking, housing networks, and kosher supervision gives leadership leverage over every life domain.


### money

- Communal economies: tuition, kosher premiums, ritual costs, wedding economies; charitable funds (gemachs) that also create dependency webs.
- In Israel: state stipends for full-time Torah study, negotiated by Haredi parties — public money sustaining the community's economic model. [OFFICIAL POLICY / GOVERNMENT REPORT]


### exit

- Among the highest exit costs of any Western religious community: leavers routinely lose spouse, children (custody battles where the community funds the observant parent), parents, siblings, employment, and having been denied secular education, marketable skills. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT / COURT RECORD: documented custody cases; org: Footsteps]
- Abuse reporting to police historically framed as mesirah (informing), with whistleblower families expelled. [COURT RECORD / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### whoBenefits

- Dynastic courts whose rebbes control institutions, real estate, and succession; communal machers brokering housing, matches, and jobs; political blocs delivering votes wholesale in exchange for state funding and regulatory autonomy (education exemptions in NY and Israel). [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT / GOVERNMENT REPORT]


### healthy

- Communities strengthening secular education and abuse reporting; internal reformers (rabbis ruling that abuse reporting is NOT mesirah); support organizations for leavers and stayers alike; the warmth, mutual aid, and low-loneliness reality that critics should honestly acknowledge.


### timeline

- 1740s–1770s — Baal Shem Tov's movement; Hasidism spreads in Eastern Europe — Charismatic rebbes create a new authority type: personal, dynastic, spiritually total.
- 1772–1800s — Vilna Gaon's opposition; Mitnagdim/Hasidic split; yeshiva movement founded — Two rival systems — dynastic charisma and scholastic elitism — both intensely authoritative.
- 1800s — Dynastic courts formalize (Satmar, Belz, Ger, Lubavitch, Bobov and others) — Succession becomes hereditary property, with institutions as the estate.
- 1881–1939 — Migration; Agudath Israel founded 1912 as political vehicle — Religious authority learns electoral politics.
- 1939–1945 — The Holocaust destroys the European heartland — Reconstruction is driven by an explicit mandate: rebuild population and insulate from the outside world.
- 1946–1970s — Rebuilding in Brooklyn, Jerusalem, Bnei Brak, Montreal, London — Total communities designed deliberately — schools, housing, employment, marriage inside one boundary.
- 1977–present — Israeli coalition politics gives Haredi parties leverage over budgets and draft exemptions — State funding sustains a full-time-study economic model. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 1990s–present — Explosive demographic growth; global Chabad emissary network — The fastest-growing Jewish segment by far.
- 2000s–present — Abuse prosecutions (Nechemya Weberman and others); mesirah taboo challenged from within — Reporting to police becomes a live internal fight. [COURT RECORD]
- 2012–present — New York yeshiva secular-education investigations; Footsteps and OTD networks grow — Education standards and exit support become public policy questions. [GOVERNMENT REPORT / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### demographics

**adherents:** Haredi population estimated ~2–2.5 million and doubling roughly every 20 years; Orthodox broadly (including Modern Orthodox) larger. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**regions:** Israel (Jerusalem, Bnei Brak, Beit Shemesh), New York (Brooklyn, Rockland, Orange counties), Montreal, London (Stamford Hill), Antwerp, Melbourne.

**branches:** Hasidic dynasties (Satmar, Ger, Belz, Vizhnitz, Chabad and many more), Litvish/yeshivish, Sephardi Haredi (Shas constituency), Modern Orthodox as a distinct and much more open category.

**trend:** Highest fertility of any Western religious group (6–7 children average in core Haredi communities); projected to reshape Jewish demography and Israeli politics within decades. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**participation:** Unlike most entries in this codex, identity and institutional participation are nearly identical here — which is exactly why exit costs are so high.


### info

- Internet filtering, banned secular media, and community bans (cherem) on specific publications or devices are documented policy in several communities. [OFFICIAL POLICY: rabbinic proclamations]
- Secular-education deficits in some boys' yeshivas — limited English, math, and science — are documented by state investigations, and constitute information control by omission. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Mesirah (the prohibition on informing to secular authorities) suppressed abuse reporting for decades; internal rulings now contest it, but social enforcement persists. [COURT RECORD / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### children

- Total-institution childhood: religious school from age 3, gender-segregated, with curriculum, dress, language (Yiddish in many communities), and marriage pathway all determined.
- Arranged introductions (shidduchim) beginning at 18–20, with family reputation determining match quality — a child's entire future depends on parental conformity. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Children of leavers are the most exposed group in this codex: custody cases in which community funds support the observant parent are documented. [COURT RECORD]
- Corporal punishment and abuse in some schools, with reporting suppressed by mesirah norms. [COURT RECORD]


### gender

- Strict gender segregation from childhood; women excluded from rabbinic authority and public religious roles.
- Modesty committees (vaad hatznius) in some communities police women's clothing, wigs, and behavior, with documented pressure campaigns against businesses and families. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- Marriage is near-universal and early; contraception typically requires rabbinic permission — reproductive decisions are institutionally mediated. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Get refusal weaponized; niddah supervision; LGBTQ members face expulsion or conversion-therapy referral. [FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### moneyTable

- Tuition, ritual costs, kosher premiums — Religious life and education — Very large family costs entrench dependence on communal aid and donors — Schools, dynastic institutions, suppliers
- Israeli state stipends for full-time study — Support Torah scholarship — Public funding sustains a model that leaves men without employable credentials — and without exit options — Institutions, political parties, the study economy [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- Gemachs (interest-free loan funds) and charity networks — Genuine mutual aid — Aid conditioned on standing; dependency webs make dissent economically fatal — Communal power brokers, and genuinely the needy
- Dynastic real estate and institutional assets — Community infrastructure — Succession fights over control of buildings and schools reveal the property nature of authority — Rebbe families and boards [COURT RECORD: dynastic litigation]


### exitTable

- Family, spouse, and children — Yes — documented — Divorce and custody proceedings where the community funds the observant parent; total shunning — “Family estrangement is their own doing.”
- Employment and housing — Yes — Jobs, housing, and credit run through the community; no secular credentials to fall back on — “Nobody fired them for leaving.”
- Education deficit — Yes — Limited secular schooling makes independent life materially difficult — “Our education is excellent — in Torah.”
- Language and social skills — Yes — Yiddish-first upbringing and cultural insulation compound isolation on exit — “That's heritage, not control.”


### whoPays

- Leavers (OTD), who lose family, children, housing, employment, and community in a single step.
- Women, under modesty policing, get refusal, and reproductive supervision.
- Abuse survivors silenced by mesirah norms and communal retaliation.
- Boys denied secular education — a lifelong economic penalty imposed before consent.
- LGBTQ community members.
- Israeli and New York taxpayers, in the narrow sense that public funds sustain the education deficits at issue.


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Low in part — Rabbinic bans, modesty rulings, and internet prohibitions are published proclamations — real receipts.
- Informal enforcement — High — Shidduch prospects, school admissions, and business boycotts do the enforcing.
- Leadership distance — High — Each dynasty and each school disclaims the others; no central Haredi authority exists.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Medium — Halachic sourcing lets any specific practice be presented as one authority's stringency.
- Cultural outsourcing — High — Custody outcomes and estrangement attributed to family dynamics rather than communal funding and pressure.
- Volunteer enforcement — High — Neighbors, mothers-in-law, and modesty committees enforce; no rebbe issues an order.
- Sacred secrecy — Low — Documented: mesirah as an explicit prohibition on external reporting. [COURT RECORD]
- Exit cost denial — High — 'Anyone can leave' — from a community that supplied every relationship, credential, and dollar.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Total-community insulation

**origin:** Rebuilt deliberately after 1945 in Brooklyn, Jerusalem, and Montreal, with explicit insulation as the design goal. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** A civilization had just been murdered. Rebuilding it required walls — against assimilation, against forgetting, against the world that had just done that. The reasoning was not paranoid; it was a response to genocide.

**expired:** Eighty years on, the walls now primarily prevent departure rather than destruction. A boy who cannot read English at sixteen is not protected from assimilation; he is prevented from leaving.

**benefitsNow:** Dynastic institutions with guaranteed populations, and political blocs delivering votes wholesale. The bill is paid by anyone inside who ever wants out.

**mechanism:** Mesirah applied to abuse allegations

**origin:** Medieval prohibition on handing Jews to gentile authorities who tortured and expropriated them. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Life-or-death protection when the outside court was the pogrom's legal arm.

**expired:** The NYPD is not a blood-libel tribunal. Applying the rule now shields the man who assaulted a child and expels the family that called it in. Internal rulings have said abuse reporting is not mesirah; social enforcement continued anyway. [COURT RECORD]

**benefitsNow:** Abusers, and institutions whose enrollment and reputation depend on silence.

**mechanism:** Secular education deficit

**origin:** Yeshiva curricula prioritizing Torah study, hardened into near-total exclusion of secular subjects in some boys' schools in the postwar rebuilding. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]

**thenPurpose:** Torah scholarship as the highest value, and a rebuilding community's need for scholars over professionals.

**expired:** A child who reaches adulthood without English literacy or arithmetic has not been given a value; he has been given a locked door. State investigations have documented the deficit. This is the mechanism that makes every other exit cost enforceable.

**benefitsNow:** The community's retention rate, directly and measurably. A man who cannot fill out a job application in English is not choosing to stay.

**mechanism:** Shidduch and modesty policing

**origin:** Arranged marriage norms and communal modesty standards, intensified by 20th-century stringency competition. [PATTERN OBSERVED]

**thenPurpose:** Matchmaking in small communities protected against unsuitable unions where families were the only information network.

**expired:** It has become a family-wide credit score. A daughter's marriage prospects depend on her brother's yeshiva, her mother's hair covering, and her father's silence — which converts every family member into an enforcer of everyone else's conformity.

**benefitsNow:** Communal power brokers who control match access, and institutions that gain enforcement without ever issuing an instruction.

### leverage

- Haredi political parties in Israel convert bloc votes into state stipends for full-time study, draft exemptions, and exemption from education standards — public money sustaining the exact curriculum deficit that makes leaving impossible. [OFFICIAL POLICY / GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- In New York, political organization has secured regulatory autonomy over yeshiva curricula while receiving substantial public funding; state investigations found many schools failing to provide basic secular instruction. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Communal charity networks (gemachs, housing help) are genuine mutual aid and simultaneously a dependency web: aid flows through standing, and standing flows through conformity. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### hardQuestions

- If Torah education is complete, why does a graduate need a community-funded charity to survive economically at thirty?
- Prominent rabbis have ruled that reporting abuse is not mesirah. Name one family in your community that reported and did not pay for it.
- Public money funds these schools. Ask why the community fights the disclosure of what is taught in them.
- When a man refuses his wife a get, which institution has ever imposed a real consequence on him? Not a statement — a consequence.
- If leaving is a personal choice, explain the community funds that appear in custody cases on one side only.
- You were taught the walls protect you. Ask honestly whether they are still facing outward.


### closing

- There are people inside your community doing this work already — rabbis who ruled that reporting is not informing, parents fighting for English literacy, mothers who chose their abused child over their standing. They did not leave. They stayed and refused. That is the model, and it is available to you.
- Nothing here asks you to stop covering your hair or to eat treif. It asks one thing: that a child in your community be able to read, and be able to tell someone, and be able to leave if he must — and that none of those three cost him his mother. If the community can give a child that, it loses nothing worth keeping.

### loopHere

**1:** Tuition, ritual costs, and communal aid circulate inside one boundary, and standing determines access at every point.

**2:** Fear of losing everything is not taught abstractly — it is demonstrated, publicly, whenever someone leaves.

**3:** The education deficit is the loop's engine: it produces adults who cannot leave, who enroll their sons in the same schools.

**4:** Bloc votes buy stipends and curriculum exemption; the exemption sustains the deficit that sustains the bloc.

**5:** Community labor builds institutions held by dynastic courts, and succession is litigated as inheritance.

**6:** An abuser is convicted, the community rallies to him, and no reporting policy is adopted.

**7:** The Holocaust and current antisemitism are real, and are invoked to make internal reform look like an attack from outside.


### chairHere

### day

**name:** Chava

**when:** A Tuesday in Cheshvan

**where:** Brooklyn


**para**

- Up at 5:40. Six children, the oldest fifteen, the youngest nine months. Lunches, uniforms, the baby on her hip while she checks that Yossi has his siddur. The apartment is loud and warm and full and she would not trade it for anything on earth, and this is important to say first because it is true.
- Yossi is thirteen. He reads Hebrew beautifully. He also cannot do long division and does not know what a continent is, and last week he asked her what a résumé was because he heard the word on a delivery man's radio. She said she would explain later. She did not explain later.
- At ten she takes the baby to the clinic and passes the shop where the sign about the modesty guidelines is taped inside the door. Two months ago the committee spoke to Devorah Feldman's husband about Devorah's wig, and then Devorah's husband lost three accounts, and nobody said the two things were connected because nobody had to.
- At two her sister calls about Malka. Malka is twenty-two and is not going to shidduchim meetings and has been seen without stockings, and the family is worried, and the way her sister says *worried* means: this will affect the younger girls. Chava says she'll talk to her. She will.
- Her cousin's son left last year. He is somewhere in Manhattan. Nobody says his name at the table, and Chava, who used to babysit him, thinks about him at odd moments — at the sink, or during candle-lighting — and then stops, because the thought does not go anywhere she can follow.
- At 11:15 the house is finally quiet. She sits at the kitchen table with tea she will not finish and thinks about Yossi and the word résumé, and then she thinks that Torah is the highest thing there is and that she believes this completely, and both thoughts are in her head at the same time, and she does not know what to do with the fact that they will not fit together.



## Hinduism
*Dharmic*


### Opening

There is no pope here, no single book, no membership roll — and you were probably told that means there is nothing to criticize. But control does not need a headquarters. It needs a family, a caste, a guru, and a birth certificate. The absence of a center is not the absence of a machine; in your tradition it is what makes the machine so hard to see.


### Overview

~1.1–1.2 billion adherents, overwhelmingly in India and Nepal; less a single religion than a civilization of paths — devotional, philosophical, ritual, ascetic — with no founder, no central text, no pope.


### Origin

Vedic religion (2nd millennium BCE onward) → Upanishadic philosophy → epic and Puranic devotionalism → medieval bhakti movements and temple economies → colonial-era reform and codification → modern guru movements and political Hindutva.


### authority

- Radically decentralized: brahmin priesthoods, temple trusts, monastic orders (mathas), gurus and godmen, caste councils, family patriarchy.
- The absence of central authority means control is local and deniable — the guru, the panchayat, the family — while the tradition as a whole disclaims responsibility. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### money

- Temple economies: India's richest temples (Tirupati, Padmanabhaswamy, Shirdi) hold assets in the billions; many major temples are administered by state governments — governments literally managing and drawing on temple wealth. [FINANCIAL RECORD / OFFICIAL POLICY: state temple endowment acts]
- Guru organizations: donation empires, ashram real estate, branded products, diaspora funding. Documented collapses (e.g., convictions of high-profile godmen for rape and murder — Ram Rahim [COURT RECORD], Asaram [COURT RECORD]) reveal internal economies of total control.
- Ritual fees, pilgrimage economies, caste-linked ritual monopolies.


### exit

- Caste operates as a birth-assigned enforcement grid; inter-caste marriage still triggers ostracism and violence in documented cases. [GOVERNMENT REPORT / COURT RECORD: honor-killing prosecutions]
- Leaving a guru movement costs the community and sometimes invested life savings; leaving Hindu identity in nationalist contexts reads as national betrayal.


### whoBenefits

- Political Hindutva: parties and movements converting religious identity into electoral majority and defining national belonging religiously. [ACADEMIC SOURCE / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- State governments administering temple funds; hereditary priesthoods with ritual monopolies; godmen with corporate empires and political protection. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### healthy

- Bhakti's own anti-clerical stream (saints who mocked priestcraft and caste); anti-caste movements from within and without (Ambedkarite critique); temple trusts with published accounts; the tradition's genuine pluralism as a resource against any single authority.


### timeline

- c. 1500–500 BCE — Vedic religion; ritual specialists; hymns transmitted orally — Priestly monopoly on ritual language — the original knowledge gatekeeping.
- c. 800–200 BCE — Upanishads; renunciant movements; Buddhism and Jainism emerge in critique — Internal dissent against sacrifice and priestcraft is present from the beginning.
- c. 200 BCE–500 CE — Dharmashastra literature (Manusmriti); epics; caste codified textually — Social hierarchy acquires scriptural sanction — the most consequential control structure in this profile.
- 500–1500 CE — Temple-building era; vast temple economies; bhakti movements — Enormous institutional wealth alongside devotional movements that explicitly reject caste and priest mediation.
- 1500–1800 — Regional kingdoms, temple patronage, matha networks — Monastic and temple institutions become durable landholders.
- 1757–1947 — Colonial rule; 'Hinduism' codified as a single religion; reform movements (Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj) — The category itself is partly a colonial administrative product. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- 1920s–1947 — Hindu nationalist organizations founded; independence and partition — Religious identity becomes a modern political project.
- 1950s–1990s — Constitutional abolition of untouchability; state temple administration; global guru movements — Legal reform proceeds while caste practice persists; Indian states take over major temple funds. [OFFICIAL POLICY]
- 1992–present — Ayodhya and the rise of Hindutva to national power — Religious majoritarianism becomes state policy. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- 2010s–present — High-profile godman convictions (Ram Rahim 2017, Asaram 2018); temple wealth disclosures — Courts document what devotion had shielded. [COURT RECORD]


### demographics

**adherents:** ~1.1–1.2 billion. [ACADEMIC SOURCE: Pew, Indian census]

**regions:** India (~1.1B), Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Indonesia (Bali), Mauritius, plus diaspora in the US, UK, Canada, South Africa, Caribbean, Gulf states.

**branches:** Vaishnava, Shaiva, Shakta, Smarta traditions; countless sampradayas, guru lineages, and regional folk forms; philosophical schools from Advaita to Dvaita.

**trend:** Growing with population; diaspora institutions expanding; Hindutva political mobilization is the major contemporary institutional development.

**participation:** There is no membership, no baptism, and no central authority — which means 'adherent' figures reflect census identity, not institutional submission. Most Hindus are under no religious hierarchy at all; control operates through caste, family, guru relationships, and temple institutions locally.


### info

- Caste-linked ritual knowledge was historically restricted by birth — Sanskrit study and Vedic recitation denied to lower castes and women, an information monopoly enforced for centuries. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- In guru movements, criticism of the guru is framed as spiritual disqualification; devotees who report abuse are labeled deluded or motivated by ego. [FORMER MEMBER TESTIMONY / COURT RECORD]
- Contemporary nationalist pressure on textbooks, films, scholars, and journalists narrows public discussion of religious history. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### children

- Samskaras from birth; thread ceremony (upanayana) for upper-caste boys; caste identity assigned at birth and legally recorded.
- Karma teaching applied to children explains inherited disadvantage as deserved — the single most efficient mechanism for producing acceptance of hierarchy. [PATTERN OBSERVED]
- Gurukula and ashram schooling has produced documented abuse cases with weak oversight. [COURT RECORD]
- Child marriage persists in some regions despite legal prohibition, defended in traditional framing. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]


### gender

- Menstrual exclusion from temples and kitchens is widespread custom; the Sabarimala litigation made it a constitutional question. [COURT RECORD: Indian Supreme Court 2018]
- Dowry is illegal and pervasive; dowry-related deaths are recorded in the thousands annually by India's own crime bureau. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Widow stigma, restrictions on remarriage in some communities, and the historical practice of sati as its extreme form. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]
- Guru sexual abuse of female devotees is documented in multiple criminal convictions. [COURT RECORD]
- Devadasi dedication of girls to temples persists illegally in some areas. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]


### moneyTable

- Temple donations, hundi collections, gold offerings — Devotion and temple upkeep — Billions in assets; state governments administer and draw on major temple funds — Temple trusts, state endowment departments, priestly establishments [FINANCIAL RECORD]
- Ritual fees and priestly services — Life-cycle rites — Hereditary monopoly pricing on birth, marriage, and death rites — Priestly families
- Guru dakshina, ashram donations, branded products — Support the guru's mission — Donation empires with no audit; convicted godmen ran corporate-scale operations — Gurus, their families, and organizational insiders [COURT RECORD]
- Pilgrimage economies (Tirupati, Kumbh, Char Dham) — Sacred travel — Priced access tiers to darshan — literally paying for a better view of God — Trusts, states, tour operators


### exitTable

- Caste standing — Yes — Birth-assigned; inter-caste marriage triggers ostracism and documented violence — “Caste is a social system, not religion.”
- Family and marriage — Yes — Honor pressure; documented honor killings prosecuted in Indian courts — “Crime, not culture.”
- Guru movement exit — Yes — Loss of community, invested savings, and years of unpaid service; labeled a traitor to the lineage — “Devotion is voluntary.”
- Spiritual threat — Yes — Karmic consequence framing; misfortune attributed to abandoning dharma — “It's just how karma works.”


### whoPays

- Dalits and lower-caste communities, bearing the tradition's oldest and largest structural harm. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]
- Women, through dowry, menstrual exclusion, widow stigma, and guru abuse.
- Inter-caste and inter-faith couples.
- Children in unregulated ashram schools.
- Devotees of convicted godmen, who lost savings and years of labor.
- Religious minorities in India, under majoritarian pressure. [INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]


### deniability

- Explicit policy — Medium — Caste has textual sanction and temple rules are written, but no central body issues doctrine.
- Informal enforcement — High — Family, caste council, and community reputation do essentially all the work.
- Leadership distance — Very high — No pope, no synod, no membership — decentralization is the strongest deniability shield in this codex.
- Doctrinal ambiguity — Very high — Any practice can be attributed to a different sampradaya, region, or era.
- Cultural outsourcing — Very high — Caste, dowry, and honor violence are all reclassified as culture, not religion.
- Volunteer enforcement — High — Panchayats, relatives, and neighbors enforce; no institution ever orders it.
- Sacred secrecy — Medium — Guru-disciple confidentiality and ashram insularity shield conduct.
- Exit cost denial — High — 'Hinduism has no dogma and no excommunication' — true institutionally, and irrelevant to the person disowned by their family.


### genealogy

**mechanism:** Caste as birth-assigned hierarchy

**origin:** Emerging in the Vedic and post-Vedic period, codified textually in Dharmashastra literature including Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE–200 CE). [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** An occupational and ritual division of labor in an agrarian society, sanctified to make it permanent and to make its permanence feel cosmic rather than political.

**expired:** Untouchability was abolished by India's constitution in 1950. Yet inter-caste marriage still triggers ostracism and documented killings, and separate temples and wells persist. A rule with no legal standing survives on social enforcement alone. [GOVERNMENT REPORT]

**benefitsNow:** Upper-caste families retaining ritual monopolies, land, and marriage networks — and every political operation that mobilizes caste blocs. The cost falls on Dalits, in the tradition's oldest and largest harm.

**mechanism:** Karma applied to inherited disadvantage

**origin:** Karma as ethical causation is ancient and philosophically serious; its application to justify caste position hardens in the classical period. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Made an otherwise indefensible social order intelligible: your position is earned, therefore just, therefore not to be resisted.

**expired:** This is the most efficient compliance mechanism ever devised, and it is applied to children. A child taught that her family's poverty is deserved learns not to ask who arranged it.

**benefitsNow:** Everyone above her in the arrangement, and no one else. Bhakti saints attacked this from within the tradition centuries ago — the internal critique is older than the colonial one.

**mechanism:** Guru surrender (guru-bhakti absolutism)

**origin:** Ancient teacher-disciple transmission, intensified in medieval sampradayas and industrialized by 20th-century global guru organizations. [ACADEMIC SOURCE]

**thenPurpose:** Oral transmission of difficult knowledge required trust and long apprenticeship in a village-scale relationship with community visibility.

**expired:** Scaled to organizations with millions of followers, real estate empires, and political protection, the same surrender means no follower has standing to question anything. Multiple godmen have been convicted of rape and murder while devotees insisted it was impossible. [COURT RECORD]

**benefitsNow:** Gurus and their families, running corporate-scale operations with donation income, no audit, and vote banks that politicians court.

**mechanism:** Temple wealth under state administration

### leverage

- Diaspora funding flows into religious-nationalist political projects, and religious identity is converted into electoral majority and a definition of who belongs to the nation. Devotion becomes constituency. [ACADEMIC SOURCE / INVESTIGATIVE REPORT]
- State governments administer major temple funds — a religious-fiscal fusion in which offerings made to a deity are budgeted by a political administration. [OFFICIAL POLICY / FINANCIAL RECORD]
- Godmen with mass followings receive political protection because their followers vote as blocs; convictions came late and only after the evidence became impossible to bury. [COURT RECORD]
- Global yoga and wellness exports generate enormous revenue for organizations and gurus, with the practice detached from any accountability structure in its source tradition. [PATTERN OBSERVED]


### hardQuestions

- Untouchability has been illegal since 1950. Ask why your village, or your family, still has two sets of cups.
- If karma explains a Dalit child's poverty, explain what it says about the family that inherited the land.
- Two godmen with tens of millions of followers were convicted of rape. Name one thing their organizations changed structurally afterward.
- Tirupati holds assets in the billions. Ask for the audited accounts. Note who tells you the question is disrespectful.
- If a guru cannot be questioned, then a guru cannot be wrong — so on what basis would you ever detect one who was?
- You were taught that caste is culture, not religion. Ask why the text that ranks people is scripture and the constitution that unranked them is not.


### closing

- The strongest critique of everything in this profile was written inside your tradition, centuries before any outsider arrived. Kabir mocked priestcraft. Basava rejected caste. Nammalvar and the bhakti poets said God does not check your birth. That lineage is yours, and it is older than the machinery.
- You do not have to stop lighting the lamp to stop funding a man. You do not have to abandon dharma to notice that someone has been selling it. Decentralization means no one can excommunicate you — which means you, more than almost any reader of this codex, are already free to refuse. The only thing holding the arrangement together is that so few people ask.
